profile.summary: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell speech to the generation that was about to enter Canaan. At the gates of the promised land, after forty years in the wilderness, Israel receives the renewal of the covenant that had already been given in Sinai. The book brings together historical remembrance, exhortation, warnings and promises, presenting the relationship between the Lord and his people as a solemn covenant, with blessings for faithfulness and judgment for disobedience. For the evangelical reader, the book highlights the seriousness of covenant obedience and God's faithfulness in conducting his redemptive work through a people called to live as a holy nation.
profile.setting: The setting is the plain of Moab, east of the Jordan, in front of Jericho, about forty years after the departure of Egypt. Israel is in transition: came out of slavery, has been preserved in the desert and is now ready to enter the promised land, but still faces powerful and hostile nations. Moses knows that he will die before leading the people beyond the Jordan, so return the terms of the covenant before entering the land. The historical background is the end of the pilgrimage in the desert and the beginning of established national life. As for authorship, the Jewish and Christian tradition attributes the book to Moses; the introduction notes that some scholars dispute this and propose later dates, although the traditional view is presented as reasonable, with possible later editorial additions, especially in the final account of Moses' death.

structure.label: Preambulo of the Alliance
structure.description: Formal presentation of the book and situation of Israel at the gates of Canaan, marking the solemn character of the renewal of the covenant.

structure.label: Historical Prologo
structure.description: Reminds the way of the people in the wilderness and the faithfulness of God until that decisive moment.

structure.label: Initial statuses and appeals
structure.description: First major section of Moses' instructions, exposing the terms of the covenant and calling the people to allegiance to the Lord.

structure.label: Estipulacoes of the Alliance
structure.description: Extensive set of commandments, guidelines and duties that regulate the life of the people as a community of covenant.

structure.label: Goods, malices and choice
structure.description: Renewal of the framework of blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience, culminating in the call to choose between life and death.

structure.label: Deposit and testimony of the covenant
structure.description: Formal closure of the pactual text, with the preservation of education and testimony against Israel.

structure.label: Lasting and Moises death
structure.description: Final word about the tribes and conclusion of the book with the death of Moses, including later editorial elements as noted in the introduction.

themes: Alliance renewed between God and Israel
Obedience as a path of blessing and disobedience as a way of judgment
Israel as a separate people to serve the Lord
Historical memory as the basis for the life of God's people
readingKeys: Notice how Moses alternates remembrance of the past, present exhortation and future hope, all connected to the covenant.
Realize the logic of blessings and curses: the book does not treat obedience as detail, but as an indispensable answer to the grace received.
Read the book as a pastoral and pactual discourse: Moses prepares the people to live as a community established on earth, and not just as pilgrims in the desert.
profile.cautions: The introduction recognizes debate about authorship and date; tradition attributes the book to Moses, but some scholars advocate later composition and additions. The reader should be careful when using the book as a basis for stiff text to date the text in a rigid way. It should also be noted that the structure is presented as an alliance text with literary form similar to ancient treatises, which helps to understand the book, but does not replace its central theological message.

dossier.narratedEra: Last month of Moses' life, with Israel encamped in the plains of Moab, on the east side of the Jordan, before Jericho, after forty years of pilgrimage in the wilderness and on the eve of the entrance to Canaan.
dossier.compositionEra: The devotional source supports the majority mosaic authorship of the book, with possible later editorial additions such as Dt 34:5-12. The introduction also records the critical proposal of dating close to the reign of Josiah, around 621 BC, and mentions possible post-exile late additions. For the final wording, a note indicates that the expression "today" in Dt 34:6 refers to the time of the final composition.

politics.title: Renewal of alliance as a political frame
politics.detail: Deuteronomy is presented as a text of suserlentness between the sovereign God and Israel, with obligations, promises and sanctions. This transforms the reading of the book: it is not only religious discourse, but a covenantal government document, in which national fidelity has public consequences.
politics.readingImpact: It helps the reader to realize that obeying is neither optional nor private; it involves the existence of the people as a community covenanted under a higher King.

politics.title: Leadership of Moses and Joshua succession
politics.detail: Moses is about to die, and Joshua has already been appointed, but has not yet been fully tested. The leadership transition is explicit in the notes, showing political and theological continuity between the great founding leader and his successor.
politics.readingImpact: The book starts to function as a power transition instruction; the future of Israel depends on correctly receiving the law before the change of leadership.

politics.title: Local authorities and Community justice
politics.detail: The notes mention chiefs in decimal structure (thousand, one hundred, fifty, ten), possibly military officers, and also judges who should not favor rich and powerful. In Dt 17, the administration of justice appears at the gates of the city, with priests or judge deciding causes.
politics.readingImpact: It shows that the alliance was applied at local levels of everyday life, and that justice was part of the political order of Israel, not just of worship.

politics.title: Monarchy allowed but regulated
politics.detail: Dept 17:15-18 presupposes the possibility of an Israelite king. The note states that the human monarchy was not contrary to the divine will, but their abuses were condemned. The king should not multiply horses, women, nor wealth, nor return to Egypt in search of military dependency.
politics.readingImpact: Reading ceases to treat royalty as something automatically bad; the focus is on the king's submission to the divine law and the rejection of merely human alliances and security.

politics.title: People and hostile powers ahead
politics.detail: The notes identify Amorites in Transjordan, with capital in Hesbon, as well as Bashã and his kings Sihon and Og. Also mentioned are Canaanites, Edomites/Seir and the threat of powerful nations in the promised territory.
politics.readingImpact: The book does not prepare the reader for a peaceful and abstract entry, but for real territorial conflict; the conquest is presented as a fulfillment of promise in the face of powers already installed.

customs.title: Form of treatise and speech of farewell
customs.detail: The work is described as a farewell speech by Moses, composed in the form of a treatise. This includes preamble, historical prologue, stipulations, blessings and curses, text deposit and witnesses.
customs.readingImpact: The reader understands that the repetition of laws is intentional and solemn, as a public renewal of commitment, not mere literary redundancy.

customs.title: Judgment in the gates of the city
customs.detail: In Dt 17, the city's door appears as a place of assemblies, trials and public executions outside the walls. The note describes a typical Israeli city as small, tight and square by the gate.
customs.readingImpact: It shows how justice was public and community practice; the law was not in the sanctuary, but in the daily civic space.

customs.title: Testimony and collective responsibility
customs.detail: The witness should cast the first stone, which prevented levian accusations and made the false testimony very serious. The punishment had a function of "purifying evil" from the community.
customs.readingImpact: It leads the reader to see the judicial process as a moral and community mechanism for the preservation of the people, not only of individual punishment.

customs.title: Sacrifice with undefective animals
customs.detail: The note on Dt 17:1 notes that a sick or defective animal had little economic value, so offering it to the Lord revealed religious contempt.
customs.readingImpact: The offering required by God involves real cost and integrity; the worship cannot be fed with no value left.

customs.title: Real marriage and accumulation of resources
customs.detail: The notes explain that ancient kings used to multiply wives for political alliances and accumulate wealth and horses as signs of power. In Israel, this would be a temptation of trust in human resources rather than God.
customs.readingImpact: The text gains a critical function of the political culture of the Ancient Near East, regulating common cutting practices and real economy.

customs.title: Pilgrimage life and community memory
customs.detail: Matthew Henry points out that the book was repeated orally and in writing to fix the memory of the new generation, as the old receivers had died. The book was also publicly read periodically, according to the introduction.
customs.readingImpact: The transmission of faith appears as continuous pedagogical practice; the national memory is cultivated by reading, repetition and public observance.

language.title: "These are the words" as an opening of alliance
language.detail: The introduction of Dt 1:1 is linked to the form of treaty documents of the Old East, which began with the identification of partners and the immediate context. This explains the solemn and legal tone of opening.
language.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the introduction is not only geographical; it establishes the legal and relational framework of the book.

language.title: Arabá, Horebe and geographical names loaded with direction
language.detail: The note explains "Arabá" as the Rift valley, and identifies Hoeb as the name used in Deuteronomy for the holy mountain of the covenant. He also comments on Horebe's possible association with "curity" or "devastation."
language.readingImpact: Geographical designations reinforce the memory of the exodus and pilgrimage; the physical scene echoes the spiritual experience of proof and revelation.

language.title: Treated and vassalage language
language.detail: The work is described as a Whiseran-vassaan treatise. The sovereign makes demands and gives promises; the vassal responds with obedience. This language shapes the understanding of alliance in Deuteronomy.
language.readingImpact: It prevents the book from being read as a mere collection of sermons; it speaks of political-legal record of covenant loyalty.

language.title: "Don't notice faces" as an image of impartiality
language.detail: In Dt 1:16-17, Hebrew is explained as "not not notice faces," an image of people with mask. The expression communicates judicial impartiality before the rich and powerful.
language.readingImpact: The metaphor helps the reader to understand that God requires judgment without favoritism, an ethics of vision without social partiality.

language.title: "Extiring evil" as a community purifying language
language.detail: In Dt 17:7, 12, the phrase "purge the evil" is explained as total removal of sin, compared to a cancer that should not remain. It is a strong language of moral sanitation of the community.
language.readingImpact: Highlight the social gravity of sin in Israel and the need for severe discipline to preserve the covenant.

language.title: Torah as "instruction" and not only "law"
language.detail: In Dt 17:18, the note explains that "torah" may refer to the book of entire Deuteronomy or at least the section of the monarchy. Matthew Henry also calls him a "second law" without implying correction of the previous one, but expansion and application.
language.readingImpact: The term extends reading: this is normative instruction for the people and their leaders, more than a cold code.

timeline.title: Departure from Sinai and long pilgrimage
timeline.detail: The introduction situates the book forty years after the exodus. The generation had received the alliance in Sinai about thirty-eight years earlier, but the rebellion led to a delay of 38 years and a tortuous path.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader sees Deuteronomy as preparation of a new generation, not as a useless repetition of the past.

timeline.title: Short path that became long delay
timeline.detail: The note states that the distance from Sinai to Kadesh-barnea was about 150 miles, a route that could be made in eleven days, but it became a decades-long because of disobedience.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology underlines the spiritual cost of rebellion and prepares the reader for the urgency of renewed obedience.

timeline.title: Moab before crossing the Jordan
timeline.detail: Israel is in the plains of Moab before Jericho, about to cross the Jordan to conquer Canaan. The location is essential to understand the tone of expectation and transition of the book.
timeline.readingImpact: Moses" speech is not abstract: it happens at the frontier of promise, when the national decision has an immediate consequence.

timeline.title: Reign of Josias as critical debate proposal
timeline.detail: The introduction records the opinion of some critical scholars that Deuteronomy would be linked to the scroll found in the temple in Josiah's time, around 621 BC, with possible post-exile additions from 538 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: Historical reading changes according to the hypothesis adopted: traditional mosaic authorship or later writing associated with reforms and exile edition.

timeline.title: Textual tradition and possible final drafting later
timeline.detail: In Dt 34:6 the expression "to this day" is linked to the time of the final composition, and Moses' death is treated as probable later editorial addition. This does not invalidate the majority mosaic authorship defended by the source, but it shows layers of writing.
timeline.readingImpact: Helps the reader to distinguish between Moses" speech and the final literary finish of the book.

timeline.title: The Late Bronze Age Treated Environment
timeline.detail: The introduction mentions Hittite texts of the late Bronze Age period, approximately 1500-1200 BC, as formal parallels closer to Deuteronomy than Assyrian treatises of the 7th century BC.
timeline.readingImpact: This is used by the source to support an ancient composition and bring the book closer to Moses' time, without fixing an exact date.

investigation: The coverage is selective: the sources provided focus mainly on introduction, Dt 1, Dt 17 and Dt 34; there are no notes attached to most of the book.

There is strong emphasis on the form of treatise, in the Moses-Josue transition and the monarchy of Dt 17, but almost nothing about economics, meals, social classes or daily worship in addition to punctual observations.
Chronological proposals appear as a mosaic tradition, Josian critical hypothesis and possible post-exile additions; the source does not definitively resolve the debate.
"Canaã," "Moab," "Arab," "Horebe" and other toponyms are explained at the geographical/literary level, not as an independent archaeological reconstruction.

Some elements are inferred by the notes such as pastoral or confessional reading (e.g. Deuteronomy as the "second law" or prefiguration of Christ), but here were used only when explicitly affirmed by the source.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends entirely on the attached notes and therefore reflects a partial coverage of the book. There is no basis here to develop important themes of Deuteronomy that do not appear in these notes. Several observations are interpretative, not independent historical evidence, especially comparisons with Hittite treatises, the critical hypothesis of dating around Josias and the mention of post-exile additions. Nor should the setting of the book be confused, located in the plains of Moab before the conquest, with the possible final composition/redaction, which the source itself distinguishes. Where the note only suggests something, this was marked as interpretation; where it mentions academic debate, it was marked as debated.
